source_text: Sed enim sepiae isti, quorum (in) figuram illud quoque pisculentum de cibis lex recusauit, ut traductionem sui sentiunt. tenebras hinc blasphemiae interuomunt atque ita intentionem uniuscuiusque iam proximam dispargunt, iactitando et adseuerando ea, quae relucentem bonitatem creatoris infuscent. sed et per istas caligines sequemur nequitiam et in lucem extrahemus ingenia tenebrarum, obicientia creatori uel maxime fraudem illam et rapinam auri et argenti, mandatam ab illo Hebraeis in Aegyptios. age, infelicissime haeretice, te ipsum expostulo arbitrum, cognosce in utramque gentem prius, et ita de auctore praecepti iudicabis. reposcunt Aegyptii de Hebraeis uasa aurea et argentea. contra Hebraei mutuas petitiones instituunt, adlegantes sibi quoque eorundem patrum nomine ex eodem scripturae instrumento mercedes restitui oportere illius operariae seruitutis pro lateris deductis, pro ciuitatibus et uillis aedificatis. quid iudicabis, optimi dei elector? Hebraeos fraudem agnoscere debere an Aegyptios compensationem? nam et aiunt ita actum per legatos utrimque, Aegyptiorum quidem repetentium uasa, Iudaeorum uero reposcentium operas suas. et tamen has iniustitia renuntiauerunt sibi Aegyptiis: hodie aduersus Marcionitas amplius adlegant Hebraei, negantes compensationi satis esse quantumuis illud auri et argenti, (si) sexcentorum milium operae per tot annos uel singulis nummis diurnis aestimentur. quae autem pars maior, repetentium uasa an incolentium uillas et urbes? querela ergo maior Aegvptiorum an gratia Hebraeorum? ut solo iniuriarum iudicio Hebraei Aegyptios repercuterent, liberi homines in ergastulum subacti, ut solas scapulas suas scribae eorum apud subsellia sua ostenderent flagellorum contumeliosa atrocitate laceratas: non paucis lancibus et scyphis pauciorum utique diuitum, sed totis ubique et ipsorum facultatibus et popularium omnium conlationibus satisfaciendum Hebraeis pronuntiassent. igitur si bona Hebraeorum causa, bona iam et causa, id est mandatum, creatoris, qui et Aegyptios gratos fecit nescientes et suum populum in tempore expeditionis angusto aliquo solatio tacitae compensationis expunxit. plane minus exigi iussit. Hebraeis enim etiam filios Aegyptii restituere debuerant.
pass_a_gloss: But indeed those cuttlefish, in whose likeness also that fish-eating of foods the law rejected, so that they may feel their own translation. From here they interrupt the darknesses of blasphemy and thus they disperse the intention of each one now next, throwing and affirming those things which darken the shining goodness of the Creator. But also through those darknesses we will follow wickedness and we will bring out into the light the talents of darkness, objecting to the Creator or especially that fraud and robbery of gold and silver, commanded by Him to the Hebrews against the Egyptians. Come, most unhappy heretic, I call you yourself as judge, recognize in which of the two nations first, and thus you will judge about the author of the command. The Egyptians demand from the Hebrews gold and silver vessels. On the other hand, the Hebrews institute mutual petitions, alleging to themselves also in the name of the same fathers from the same scriptural instrument that wages ought to be restored to them for that servile work for the bricks deducted, for the cities and villages built. What will you judge, chooser of the best God? Ought the Hebrews to acknowledge fraud or the Egyptians compensation? For they also say that it was done thus through legates on both sides, indeed the Egyptians demanding vessels, but the Jews demanding their own works. And yet the Egyptians renounced these injustices to themselves: today the Hebrews will allege more against the Marcionites, denying that compensation is sufficient however much that gold and silver, if the work of six hundred thousand through so many years or single daily coins is estimated. But which part is greater, of those demanding vessels or of those inhabiting villages and cities? Is the complaint therefore greater of the Egyptians or the gratitude of the Hebrews? So that by the sole judgment of injuries the Hebrews may repel the Egyptians, free men subjected to a workhouse, so that they may show only their own shoulders to their scribes at their benches lacerated by the contemptuous atrocity of whips: not with a few platters and cups of a few wealthy men, but with all and everywhere and the contributions of all the people it would have been necessary to satisfy the Hebrews. Therefore if the cause of the Hebrews is good, the cause, that is the command, of the Creator is also good, who made the Egyptians grateful unknowingly and outlined His own people in the time of the expedition with some solace of silent compensation. Clearly He commanded less to be exacted. For the Hebrews ought to have restored also the sons of the Egyptians.

bible_refs.note: Hebrews demanding gold and silver vessels

pass_b_english: Those cuttlefish, in whose likeness the law also rejected that fish-eating of foods so they might feel their own translation, vomit up darknesses of blasphemy from here and so scatter the intention of each one now at hand, throwing out and affirming the very things that darken the shining goodness of the Creator. Yet even through those darknesses we will track wickedness and drag the talents of darkness into the light, charging the Creator with—most of all—that fraud and robbery of gold and silver which He commanded the Hebrews to commit against the Egyptians (Exodus 12:35-36). Come, most unhappy heretic, I call you yourself to be the judge: recognize which of the two nations acted first, and then you will pass judgment on the author of the command. The Egyptians demand gold and silver vessels back from the Hebrews. The Hebrews, for their part, file counter-petitions, citing the same scriptural authority in the name of the same fathers to claim that wages ought to be restored to them for that servile labor—the bricks deducted, the cities and villages built. What will you judge, chooser of the best God? Must the Hebrews admit fraud, or the Egyptians pay compensation? For they also say it was handled thus through envoys on both sides: the Egyptians demanding their vessels, the Jews demanding their labor. And yet the Egyptians renounced those injustices against themselves. Today the Hebrews will allege even more against the Marcionites, denying that compensation is sufficient no matter how much gold and silver, if the labor of six hundred thousand over so many years is reckoned even at single daily coins. But which side carries the greater claim—those demanding vessels, or those inhabiting villages and cities? Is the grievance therefore greater for the Egyptians, or the debt of gratitude for the Hebrews? So that by the sole judgment of injuries the Hebrews might repel the Egyptians—free men forced into a workhouse, so that they might show only their own shoulders to their overseers at their benches, lacerated by the contemptuous atrocity of whips—not with a few platters and cups from a few wealthy men, but with everything, everywhere, and the contributions of all the people, it would have been necessary to satisfy the Hebrews. Therefore if the Hebrews' cause is good, the cause—that is, the command—of the Creator is also good, who made the Egyptians grateful without their knowing it and marked out His own people in the time of the exodus with some solace of silent compensation. Clearly He commanded less to be exacted. For the Hebrews ought to have restored the sons of the Egyptians as well.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass B correctly identifies the implied biblical context (Exodus 12:35-36) for the robbery of gold and silver, which is required for scripture identification. Pass A and B are consistent with the Latin source.

Pass B: 'He commanded the Hebrews to commit against the Egyptians (Exodus 12:35-36)' matches the source's reference to 'mandatam ab illo Hebraeis in Aegyptios' and the note identifies 'Hebrews demanding gold and silver vessels' as the basis for the citation. Pass A: 'the law rejected, so that they may feel their own translation' matches 'lex recusauit, ut traductionem sui sentiunt.'
